newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK producer price data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK producer price data.

text.p: Following is a list of analysts' reactions to UK producer data published at 0830 GMT.
* UK APRIL OUTPUT PRICES +0.2% MM,+0.8% YY,INPUT PRICES YY -10.5%,S/A -1.9% MM (VS expectations +0.1, +0.8 -8.4, -0.5)
* UK APRIL S/A OUTPUT PRICES EX FDTP +0.1% MM, +0.5% Y/Y

UNION PLC ECONOMIST PHILIP SHAW - "Obviously the scale of the decrease is a bit of a surprise but we did have quite a sharp appreciation of sterling over the month of April and we saw oil prices coming down in dollar terms too."

"One factor tempering the decline in headline output price inflation will be the fact that earnings growth is fairly strong in the manufacturing sector as well. Figures that we've seen for February show earnings growth at 4-3/4 percent and that's got to be factored into the costs borne by manufacturers as well," Shaw added.

PETER LUXTON, CHIEF ECONOMIC ADVISER MMS INTERNATIONAL - "I think what you're finding between that (the input prices) and the output price story is now that the margin building story is creeping back in again. Firms are now rebuilding their profit margins to take advantage of the lower input prices -- not to pass it on but to rebuild profits."

DAVID BLOOM, JAMES CAPEL ECONOMIST - "The output side of things in bang in line with expectations -- that's not a surprise. But the input prices came as a surprise. The combination of sterling and falling oil prices has been responsible for the fall in input prices.

If there were to be any signs of inflation it wouldn't be from the input side, it would be demand pull inflation. This is another positive for the gilt market -- after a blistering run, it can hold on to its gains."

BANK OF AMERICA ECONOMIST JEREMY HAWKINS - "The UK PPI data are soft across the board and boost the likelihood that inflation will fall below the government's 2.5 per cent target over coming months. The main focus is the core Output Price Index which rose just 0.1 per cent last month. This left the year on year rate steady at a subdued 0.5 per cent and confirms an absence of non-labour cost pressures in manufacturing industry. Moreover the sharper than expected slide in input prices - now down a whopping 10.5 per cent at an annual rate - makes for a very soft external picture too. Should be well received by gilts and more reason for expecting no rate hike next month. To this end, a small negative for the pound."
